t: Minimum Number of String Groups Through Transformations
o: A transformation independently cyclically rotates the even-index characters and the odd-index characters of a string. Strings in one group must be mutually transformable into each other, and we want the fewest groups — i.e., the number of equivalence classes. Equivalence is captured by a canonical form: the lexicographically smallest rotation of the even subsequence concatenated with that of the odd subsequence; two strings are equivalent iff their canonical forms match. Example 2 yields 3 classes, Example 3 yields 5.
k: Canonical form = min-rotation(E) + separator + min-rotation(O); group count = number of distinct canonical forms.
Naively trying all rotations costs O(L^2) per string; Booth's algorithm finds the least rotation in O(L), essential since one word can be 5e5 characters.

a.i: Split each word into its even and odd subsequences, generate every cyclic rotation of each, and take the lexicographically smallest combination as the key. Hash the keys and return the number of distinct keys. Simple and obviously correct, but generating all L rotations of an L-length piece costs O(L^2), which can hit ~2.5e11 operations for a single 5e5-character word.
s: For each word, extract E = chars at even indices and O = chars at odd indices.
Compute min over all rotations of E and of O; key = minE + '|' + minO.
Insert keys into a set; return its size.
a.t: O(sum L_i^2) time — each string generates all rotations of its halves; fine for short words but can TLE on one 5e5-char word; O(sum L_i) space.
a.sp: O(sum L_i) — the hash set of canonical keys.

a.n: Approach 2: Booth's algorithm for least rotation (optimal)
a.i: Booth's algorithm computes the starting index of the lexicographically least rotation in O(L) using a failure-function-style scan over s+s. Applying it to E and O separately gives canonical forms in linear total time, comfortably handling the 5e5 length bound.
s: Implement Booth's least-rotation index on s+s with an auxiliary failure array.
Key each word as minrot(E) + '|' + minrot(O).
Count distinct keys with a hash set.
a.t: O(sum L_i) time — Booth's algorithm is linear per string, hashing adds expected linear cost; O(sum L_i) space.
a.sp: O(sum L_i) — doubled strings during scanning plus the key set.

w: Always land on Booth's algorithm (or Duval/least-rotation via suffix comparisons) given the 5e5 total-length bound; the brute force is only for explanation. Key insight to articulate: independent rotations of E and O mean equivalence is exactly 'same multiset structure with matching minimal rotations', so a canonical-form hash solves grouping in one pass. Pitfalls: odd/even extraction off-by-one, forgetting a separator between the two rotated halves (ambiguous concatenation), and O(L^2) substring churn in Java. Edge cases: length-1 words (each its own class unless duplicates), and words differing only in parity placement. Follow-up: allow swapping E and O, or count pairs of equivalent words.
